facts.subject: science
facts.text: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. Since 1983 it has been fixed by definition, and the meter is defined from it.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water, which is why it floats. In almost every other substance, the solid form is denser than the liquid.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth. Astronomers spotted it in sunlight in 1868, and it was not isolated on Earth until 1895.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Gallium is a metal that melts at about 29.8 °C, below human body temperature, so a solid lump of it can melt in your hand.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Diamond and graphite (the 'lead' in pencils) are both made of pure carbon. Only the arrangement of their atoms is different.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Old church windows that are thicker at the bottom did not flow over the centuries. Glass at room temperature would take longer than the age of the universe to sag; the panes were simply made unevenly.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Air heated by a lightning bolt can reach about 50,000 °F, roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Lightning can strike as far as 10 miles away from a thunderstorm, which is about as far as you can normally hear thunder.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Humans and chimpanzees differ by only about 1.2% in the DNA of the genes they share.
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Its old Greek-derived name, hydrargyrum, means 'liquid silver', which is where its symbol Hg comes from.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,414 °C. Its chemical symbol is W because of its other name, wolfram.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Scientists estimate that roughly 68 to 70% of the universe is dark energy, a mysterious force that seems to be speeding up the universe's expansion.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Dark matter, which cannot be seen directly, is thought to make up about 85% of all the matter in the universe.

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Individual humans differ from each other by only about 0.1% of their DNA, on average.
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

facts.subject: science
facts.text: Sound travels much faster through water than it does through air.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, can reach about 2 million °C, while its visible surface is a comparatively cool 5,500 °C.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Energy made in the Sun's core takes about 170,000 years to travel out to the top of its convection zone.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: The Sun does not spin as one solid ball. It rotates once every 25 Earth days at its equator but takes about 36 days near its poles.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: About 30 Earth-sized planets could fit in the gap between Earth and the Moon.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about an inch (2.5 cm) every year.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Apollo astronauts brought back 382 kilograms (842 pounds) of Moon rocks and soil, which scientists are still studying today.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days).

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Venus spins backward compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: The surface of Venus reaches about 467 °C, hot enough to melt lead, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In theory, it would float in a big enough bathtub.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Saturn's rings stretch up to 282,000 km from the planet, yet the main rings are typically only about 10 meters thick.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Jupiter has the shortest day in the solar system: it spins once in about 9.9 hours.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm about twice as wide as Earth, and it has been observed for more than 300 years.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Mars is home to Valles Marineris, a canyon system about 3,870 km long, the largest canyon in the solar system.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Mars is only about half as wide as Earth, but its total surface area is nearly the same as all of Earth's dry land.

facts.subject: space
facts.text: Sunlight takes about 13 minutes to travel from the Sun to Mars.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Earth is the only planet whose English name doesn't come from Greek or Roman mythology. The name is Germanic and simply means 'the ground'.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Measured from its base on the sea floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest, but most of it is underwater.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Earth's longest mountain range is underwater. It is about four times longer than the Andes, Rockies and Himalayas combined.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Earth's inner core can reach about 5,400 °C, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: The North American tectonic plate moves west at roughly the same rate that your fingernails grow.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Earth's magnetic field flips (north becomes south) about every 300,000 years on average, though the timing is irregular.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: About 96.5% of all the water on Earth is in the oceans.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow hold about 68.7% of all of Earth's fresh water.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: About half of the oxygen on Earth is produced in the ocean, mostly by tiny drifting plankton.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Prochlorococcus, the smallest photosynthetic organism on Earth, produces up to 20% of the oxygen in the entire biosphere.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: The ocean's average depth is about 3,682 meters, and its deepest known point, the Challenger Deep, is about 10,935 meters down.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth. It stretches about 2,300 km and is made of nearly 3,000 individual reefs.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: Earth is the only planet in our solar system known to have liquid water on its surface.

facts.subject: earth
facts.text: At any one time, about 3,100 cubic miles of water are floating in the atmosphere, mostly as invisible water vapor.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Scientists estimate that Greenland sharks live at least 250 years, and possibly more than 500.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: A sea turtle's sex is set by temperature: eggs incubated below about 27.7 °C hatch as males, and eggs above about 31 °C hatch as females.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Horseshoe crabs aren't true crabs. They are more closely related to spiders and scorpions, and their blood is used to test vaccines and medical devices for bacteria.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: The bowhead whale is the longest-lived marine mammal and may live for more than 200 years.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: The largest fish in the sea is the whale shark, which may grow up to 40 feet (12 m) long.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Starfish aren't fish. Scientists prefer the name 'sea stars', and these animals can regrow a lost arm.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, and males have venomous spurs on their hind feet.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Penguins can't fly, but their wings are built for swimming, letting some species reach 15 to 25 miles per hour underwater.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: The Australian box jellyfish is considered the most venomous marine animal.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: The blue whale is the most massive animal known to have ever lived.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as a human. Each one is just much longer.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Wombats produce cube-shaped poo. Scientists found that stiff and flexible sections of their intestine shape it into cubes.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Tiny animals called tardigrades, or water bears, survived 10 days exposed to the vacuum of open space on a 2007 European space mission.

facts.subject: animals
facts.text: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, able to sprint at about 60 to 70 miles per hour in short bursts.
facts.sourceName: Live Science, citing the Smithsonian's National Zoo

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Babies are born with about 270 bones. Many fuse together as they grow, leaving adults with about 206.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: The smallest bone in your body is the stapes in your middle ear. It is about 3 mm long and shaped like a stirrup.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: A study estimated that the human nose can tell apart more than 1 trillion different smells.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, which adds up to more than 2.6 billion beats over an average lifetime.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your heart pumps blood through about 60,000 miles (96,000 km) of blood vessels.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your brain makes up about 2% of your body weight but uses around 20% of its energy, running on roughly 20 watts.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, even harder than bone.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: The liver can regrow. If part of a healthy liver is removed, the rest can grow back to about its original size.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: The cornea, the clear front of your eye, has no blood vessels. It gets its oxygen directly from the air.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your skin is your body's largest organ.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month, more than twice as fast as toenails (about 1.6 mm a month).

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells, not the 10-to-1 ratio once claimed.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: A red blood cell lives for about 110 to 120 days before it is removed, mostly by the spleen.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: Your left lung is slightly smaller than your right because the heart takes up some room on the left side.

facts.subject: body
facts.text: The right lung has three lobes, but the left lung has only two, with a notch where the heart fits.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Botanically, bananas are berries but strawberries are not.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Peanuts aren't true nuts. They are legumes, related to peas and beans, and they ripen underground.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Vanilla comes from the pods of an orchid. It is the second most expensive spice after saffron because growing it takes so much hand labor.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Tomatoes come from the Americas. They reached Italy in the 1500s, but tomato sauce didn't become an Italian staple until the late 1700s.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: The potato was first domesticated in the Andes mountains of South America.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Birds don't feel the burn of chili peppers. Capsaicin doesn't trigger their pain receptors, so they eat the peppers and spread the seeds.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Honey lasts so long because it is very low in moisture and quite acidic (a pH of about 3 to 4.5), which makes it hard for microbes to survive.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: The ingredient that makes some peanut butter easier to spread, carrageenan, comes from red seaweed.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Bananas are very slightly radioactive because of their natural potassium. You'd need to eat about 100 bananas to match the natural radiation you get each day.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Saffron is made from the tiny stigmas of crocus flowers. It takes about 75,000 flowers to make one pound of the spice.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: A cashew nut grows on the outside of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple, and its shell contains an oil that can blister skin.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: Rice is the staple food for more than half of the world's population.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: A pineapple plant usually takes 18 to 24 months to produce its fruit, and each plant gives just one pineapple at a time.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: The Aztecs used cacao beans as money. In the 1500s, about 100 cacao beans could buy a turkey.

facts.subject: food
facts.text: The oldest known traces of cacao use, about 5,300 years old, were found in the upper Amazon in Ecuador, not in Mexico or Central America.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Russia is the largest country in the world and stretches across 11 time zones.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Canada has the longest coastline of any country, largely thanks to the 36,000-plus islands of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Siberia's Lake Baikal is the world's deepest and oldest lake, and it holds about one-fifth of all the fresh water on Earth's surface.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the constitutional capital, while La Paz is the seat of government.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, is the highest national capital in the world, sitting more than 3,000 meters above sea level.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Vatican City is the world's smallest country, covering just 0.44 square kilometers.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Indonesia is made up of roughly 17,500 islands, and more than 7,000 of them are uninhabited.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest waterfall, dropping a total of 979 meters.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: The surface of the Dead Sea is the lowest body of water on Earth's surface, more than 400 meters below sea level.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: The Pacific Ocean got its name from explorer Ferdinand Magellan in 1520. 'Pacific' means peaceful, after the calm water he found there.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Lesotho is one of only three countries completely surrounded by another country (along with Vatican City and San Marino), and its lowest point is about 1,400 meters above sea level.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Only about a quarter of the Sahara is covered in sand. Most of the rest is rocky plains, plateaus and mountains.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Chile's Atacama Desert is so dry that some of its weather stations have never recorded a single drop of rain.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: Istanbul sits on both sides of the Bosporus strait, so part of the city is in Europe and part is in Asia.

facts.subject: geography
facts.text: The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert, covering about 8.6 million square kilometers across North Africa.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Woolly mammoths survived on Siberia's Wrangel Island until about 4,300 years ago, after the first Egyptian pyramids had already been built.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree from 196 BCE in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. That is what let scholars finally decode hieroglyphs.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Most delegates signed the U.S. Declaration of Independence on August 2, 1776, not July 4. July 4 is when its wording was approved.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Machu Picchu was probably built in the mid-1400s, likely as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure in the world for an estimated 3,800 years.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Tree rings show that Vikings were cutting wood in Newfoundland, Canada, in the year 1021, more than 470 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, completed in 537, was the largest cathedral in the Christian world for almost a thousand years.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted no more than about 40 minutes, making it the shortest war in recorded history.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Berlin Wall went up overnight on August 12-13, 1961, and stood for 28 years until it was opened on November 9, 1989.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Gutenberg Bible, finished in Mainz around 1455, was the first major book in Europe printed with movable metal type.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is the Korean Buddhist text known as Jikji, printed in 1377, 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: The Hundred Years' War between England and France actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces in between.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 largely intact. Removing and recording its contents took about a decade.

facts.subject: history
facts.text: Between 1949 and 1961, before the Berlin Wall was built, about 2.5 million East Germans fled to the West.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Christianity is the world's largest religion, with about 2.3 billion followers in 2020, roughly 29% of the world's population.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Between 2010 and 2020, Islam was the fastest-growing major religious group, reaching about a quarter of the world's population.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: In 2020, about 24% of people worldwide had no religious affiliation, making the religiously unaffiliated the third-largest group after Christians and Muslims.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: In the original Greek myth, Pandora opened a jar, not a box. It became a 'box' in the 16th century, probably through a mistranslation.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Thursday is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder, and Wednesday after Woden (Odin).

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Japan's Ise Grand Shrine, the most sacred Shinto shrine, is rebuilt from scratch every 20 years, a tradition dating back to the late 600s.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan moves through every season over roughly 33 years.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: In ancient Egyptian belief, the heart of a dead person was weighed against the feather of Maat, goddess of truth, to judge whether they could enter the afterlife.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Western Christian Easter can fall on any Sunday from March 22 to April 25, because its date is based on the first full moon on or after March 21.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: The Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, India, marks the place where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Uranus is the only planet named after a Greek god rather than a Roman one. Earth is the only planet not named after a god at all.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: January is named after Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who was often shown with two faces looking in opposite directions.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak, who was born in 1469 in a village near Lahore in present-day Pakistan.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: In Norse mythology, Yggdrasil is a giant ash tree that holds the universe together and connects the nine worlds, including Asgard and Midgard.

facts.subject: religion
facts.text: Hanukkah lasts eight days and commemorates the rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem in the 160s BCE.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: The United Nations officially came into existence on 24 October 1945, which is why 24 October is celebrated as UN Day.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: The United Nations has 193 member states. The newest is South Sudan, admitted in 2011.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Iceland's parliament, the Althing, was founded around the year 930, making it one of the oldest national parliaments in the world.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Voting has been compulsory in Australian federal elections since 1924, and turnout has never fallen below 90% since then.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: The European Union has 24 official languages, which makes 552 possible language pairs for translation.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: In 2007, Estonia became the first country to let people vote over the internet in a national parliamentary election.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Switzerland is governed by a seven-member Federal Council. Each year one of the seven serves as President of the Confederation.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: The United Kingdom has no single written constitution. Its rules are spread across laws, court rulings, conventions and historic documents.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: India's 2024 general election was the largest election in history: about 642 million people voted, over seven phases lasting six weeks.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Only three clauses of the Magna Carta (first sealed in 1215) are still part of the law in England and Wales today.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: In 2007, Austria became the first country in the European Union to lower the voting age to 16 for all elections.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Brazil lowered its voting age to 16 for all elections, including presidential ones, back in 1988.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: To become President of the United States, a person must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and have lived in the U.S. for at least 14 years.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: King Charles III is head of state of 15 countries, known as Commonwealth realms, including the UK, Canada, Australia and Jamaica.

facts.subject: politics
facts.text: Bhutan's 2008 constitution makes Gross National Happiness a goal of the state, an idea credited to its fourth king in the 1970s.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world where women could vote in parliamentary elections.
facts.sourceName: NZ Ministry for Culture and Heritage

facts.subject: society
facts.text: In New Zealand's first election with women voters (1893), about 82% of enrolled women voted, a higher turnout than men's of about 70%.
facts.sourceName: NZ Ministry for Culture and Heritage

facts.subject: society
facts.text: In 1906, Finland became the first country in Europe to give women both the right to vote and the right to run for parliament. In 1907, 19 women were elected.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) became the world's first woman prime minister in 1960.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: In 2025, women held about 27% of seats in national parliaments worldwide, up from about 11% in 1995.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: Rwanda has the world's highest share of women in parliament: in 2025, women held about 64% of seats in its lower chamber.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: Women in Switzerland gained the right to vote in national elections in 1971, after a nationwide referendum.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: In 1974, Sweden became the first country to introduce paid parental leave that both mothers and fathers could take.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: The world's population reached 8 billion people on 15 November 2022, according to the United Nations.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: It took about 12 years for the world's population to grow from 7 billion to 8 billion. The UN projects it will peak at around 10.4 billion in the 2080s.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: Women outlive men in every part of the world, according to the World Health Organization.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: About 55% of the world's people live in cities and towns, and the UN expects that to reach 68% by 2050. In 1950 it was only 30%.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: The United Nations first celebrated International Women's Day on 8 March 1975, during International Women's Year.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: At least 739 million adults worldwide still cannot read and write, and about two-thirds of them are women.

facts.subject: society
facts.text: New Zealand's 1893 voting law included Māori women as well, who voted for the Māori seats in Parliament.
facts.sourceName: NZ Ministry for Culture and Heritage

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Marie Curie is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Albert Einstein's Nobel Prize was not for relativity. It was awarded for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Abraham Lincoln is the only U.S. president to hold a patent: an 1849 invention for lifting boats over shallow water.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Leonardo da Vinci filled his notebooks with mirror writing, running from right to left.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Isaac Newton spent the last 30 years of his life running England's Royal Mint and personally pursued counterfeiters.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963, orbiting Earth 48 times in about 71 hours aboard Vostok 6.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Beethoven was profoundly deaf by the time his Ninth Symphony premiered in 1824. At the end he had to be turned around to see the audience applauding.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: In 1932, Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, crossing in about 15 hours.
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Malala Yousafzai was 17 when she was awarded the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize, making her the youngest Nobel laureate ever.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961. His flight on Vostok 1 lasted 108 minutes.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Yuri Gagarin wasn't allowed to fly his own spacecraft. Ground crews controlled Vostok 1, because nobody yet knew how weightlessness would affect a person.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first confirmed climb to the summit of Mount Everest on 29 May 1953.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: In January 1610, Galileo discovered Jupiter's four largest moons, now called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison. Four years after his release he became South Africa's first democratically elected president, in 1994.

facts.subject: people
facts.text: Of the 143 paintings Frida Kahlo created, 55 are self-portraits.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The Wright brothers' first powered flight, on 17 December 1903, lasted just 12 seconds and covered 120 feet (36 m).
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: Bluetooth is named after Harald 'Bluetooth', a 10th-century Danish king credited with uniting Denmark. The logo combines his initials in ancient runes.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The first product ever scanned with a barcode was a pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and chose the @ sign for addresses because it was rarely used and meant 'at'.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The oldest surviving photograph, taken by Nicéphore Niépce around 1826-27, needed an exposure of at least eight hours.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: Velcro was inspired by burrs. Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed how they stuck to his dog's fur after a walk in 1941.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, and the first website ran at info.cern.ch.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: On 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web's software royalty-free so anyone could use it, which helped the Web spread around the world.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The first text message, sent on 3 December 1992, simply said 'Merry Christmas'.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: In 1854, Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety elevator in New York by having the rope holding his platform cut. The safety brake caught it.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The QWERTY keyboard layout comes from typewriters of the 1870s and appears in an 1878 patent by Christopher Latham Sholes.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The Concorde airliner cruised at more than twice the speed of sound and could fly from London to New York in roughly three to three and a half hours. It retired in 2003.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), roughly 8 kilometers every second.

facts.subject: technology
facts.text: A standard text message (SMS) is limited to 160 characters, including spaces.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: In 1843, Ada Lovelace published a method for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: Ada Lovelace wrote that the Analytical Engine 'has no pretensions whatever to originate anything': it could only do what it was instructed to do.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: In 1947, engineers found a real moth stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer and taped it into the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined by John McCarthy in a 1955 proposal for a summer research workshop at Dartmouth in 1956.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue became the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match under tournament conditions.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: Deep Blue could evaluate about 200 million chess positions per second, using 256 processors working together.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers (1945), weighed about 30 tons and filled a 30-by-50-foot room.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: ENIAC was first programmed by six women, including Jean Jennings Bartik and Betty Snyder Holberton, who had been hired to calculate trajectories during World War II.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for discoveries that made machine learning with artificial neural networks possible.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul. More than 200 million people watched.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: AlphaGo's famous 'Move 37' against Lee Sedol was so unusual that DeepMind estimated a human would play it only 1 time in 10,000. Commentators first thought it was a mistake.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: The first computer mouse, built at SRI in 1964, had a wooden shell and a single button.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: Douglas Engelbart, who invented the computer mouse, never received any royalties for it.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: One of the first chatbots, ELIZA, was built at MIT in the mid-1960s. Its best-known script imitated a therapist by turning your sentences back into questions.

facts.subject: ai
facts.text: CAPTCHA stands for 'Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart'. It was invented at Carnegie Mellon University around 2000.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: There are about 7,170 living languages in the world today.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: Papua New Guinea has more languages than any other country: about 840 living languages.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: The word 'robot' comes from a 1920 Czech play by Karel Čapek. It is based on 'robota', meaning forced labor.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: 'Ampersand' comes from schoolchildren reciting the alphabet: the & at the end was read as 'and per se and', which got squashed into one word.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: 'Emoji' has nothing to do with 'emotion'. It comes from the Japanese e (picture) and moji (character).

facts.subject: language
facts.text: On the Canary Island of La Gomera, people can 'speak' Spanish entirely in whistles. The whistled language, Silbo Gomero, is on UNESCO's cultural heritage list.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created on purpose by King Sejong and his scholars in 1443 to make reading easier for ordinary people.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: South Korea celebrates Hangul Day every 9 October, the anniversary of the alphabet's proclamation in 1446.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: 'Quarantine' comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, 'forty days': how long ships from plague areas had to wait before landing.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: 'OK' first appeared in print in a Boston newspaper in 1839 as a joke abbreviation of 'oll korrect', a deliberate misspelling of 'all correct'.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: The dot over a lowercase i or j has a name: it's called a tittle.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: 'Goodbye' is a shortened form of 'God be with ye', a parting phrase used in the 1500s.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: More than 70 million deaf people around the world use more than 300 different sign languages.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: Basque, spoken in parts of Spain and France, is a 'language isolate': linguists have found no other language related to it.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: Esperanto was invented in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof. Its name comes from his pen name, which means 'one who hopes'.

facts.subject: language
facts.text: The Hawaiian alphabet has just 13 letters: five vowels, seven consonants and the ʻokina, a glottal stop.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by a former museum worker and was missing for over two years. The theft helped make it the world's most famous painting.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Before it was stolen in 1911, the Mona Lisa wasn't even the most famous painting in its own gallery. When it returned, more than 100,000 people came to see it in two days.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in caves in southwestern Germany, are about 35,000 years old: some of the oldest known musical instruments.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: A cave painting in Sulawesi, Indonesia, showing human-like figures with a wild pig, is at least 51,200 years old: the oldest known example of a painted story.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The Eiffel Tower was only supposed to stand for 20 years after the 1889 World's Fair.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Gustave Eiffel saved his tower from demolition by turning it into a giant antenna for radio and scientific experiments.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Michelangelo didn't paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling lying on his back. He stood on scaffolding, craning his neck upward, from 1508 to 1512.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The Statue of Liberty was originally copper-brown like a new penny. It took about 30 years for its green patina to form.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The note names do, re, mi come from an 11th-century hymn: the monk Guido of Arezzo used the first syllable of each line (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la).

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The Hollywood sign was built in 1923 as an advertisement for a housing development and originally read 'HOLLYWOODLAND'.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The dome of Rome's Pantheon, nearly 2,000 years old, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: The Taj Mahal was built between about 1632 and 1648 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Hokusai's 'The Great Wave' is a woodblock print, not a single painting. Experts estimate up to 8,000 copies were printed.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Violin maker Antonio Stradivari made more than 1,100 instruments, and about 650 of them survive today.

facts.subject: arts
facts.text: Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream: two paintings, two pastels and around 30 lithograph prints.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: When Pierre de Coubertin designed the Olympic rings in 1913, every national flag contained at least one of its six colours (five rings plus the white background).

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: The colours of the Olympic rings don't stand for particular continents. That is a common misconception, says the IOC.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: From 1912 to 1948, the Olympics awarded medals for art: architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics, won an Olympic gold medal for literature in 1912 with his 'Ode to Sport', submitted under a pen name.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: The marathon's odd length of 42.195 km dates from the 1908 London Olympics, when the route ran from Windsor Castle to the royal box in the stadium.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: In 1971, astronaut Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14. They are still there.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Basketball was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, and the first goals were two peach baskets nailed 10 feet up.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Volleyball was invented in 1895 by William G. Morgan, and its original name was 'Mintonette'.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Tug of war was an Olympic sport at five Games, from 1900 until 1920.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Usain Bolt's 100 m world record of 9.58 seconds, set in Berlin in 2009, cut the record by the biggest margin in history.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: The first modern Olympic Games, in Athens in 1896, had 241 athletes from 14 nations.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Women first competed at the Olympics in Paris in 1900: 22 of the 997 athletes.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: British tennis player Charlotte Cooper became the first woman to win an individual Olympic title, at Paris 1900.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: The first FIFA World Cup, in 1930, was hosted and won by Uruguay. Only 13 teams took part.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: The Paralympics grew from a 1948 archery contest for injured veterans at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England. The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960.

facts.subject: sports
facts.text: Wimbledon, first held in 1877, is the oldest of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments and the only one still played on grass.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Despite the popular claim, the Great Wall of China is generally not visible to the naked eye from orbit. It is long but far too narrow.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: The Eiffel Tower grows slightly in summer as its iron expands in the heat, and it even leans a little away from the Sun.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. All three landed safely.
facts.sourceName: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Sharks are older than trees. Sharks have been around for roughly 400 to 450 million years, while the first trees appeared about 350 million years ago.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Standing on Mars at the equator at noon, your feet could feel like spring (about 24 °C) while your head is at freezing (about 0 °C).

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: If the Sun were as tall as a typical front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Jupiter is so big that about 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: In 1989, an eruption on the Sun triggered a magnetic storm that left 6 million people in Canada without power for 9 hours.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Mars's moon Phobos is slowly spiraling inward. In about 50 million years it will crash into Mars or break apart.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Mars's volcano Olympus Mons rises more than 25 miles (40 km) from base to summit, far taller than Mount Everest.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Venus has a tiny travelling companion: a quasi-moon called Zoozve, estimated at 200 to 500 meters across.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: The Moon's surface swings from about 127 °C in sunlight to about -173 °C in darkness.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: As many as 10 million jets of gas called spicules can burst from the Sun's surface at once, some moving at 60 miles per second.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: The original Hollywoodland sign was lit by 4,000 light bulbs that flashed 'HOLLY', then 'WOOD', then 'LAND'.

facts.subject: fun
facts.text: Venus's axis is tilted only about 3 degrees, so unlike Earth it has no real seasons.
